findings.statement: At 16:52:33 BST three almost simultaneous lightning strikes were recorded adjacent to the Eaton Socon–Wymondley 400 kV circuit, close to Willian Arboretum at the Wymondley end; any of the three could have hit the circuit (largest 33.7 kA).

The initiating event was a single-phase (blue phase) to earth fault on one Eaton Socon–Wymondley 400 kV circuit at 16:52:33.490 BST, about 4.5 km from Wymondley Main; NGET attributes the fault to a lightning strike.
Main protection at the Wymondley Main end cleared the fault 70 ms after inception (circuit end open at 16:52:33.560 BST).
Main protection at the Eaton Socon end cleared the fault 74 ms after inception (circuit end open at 16:52:33.564 BST).

Both clearance times are within the 80 ms primary-protection clearance time required at 400 kV (Grid Code CC.6.2.3.1.1, as cited by NGET); NGET and the ESO report assess that the transmission protection operated as designed.

Delayed auto-reclose re-energised the Eaton Socon–Wymondley circuit at 16:52:53 BST, about 20 s after the fault, leaving the network in its pre-event configuration with no further operational intervention.

The 16:52:53 reclose was the designed auto-reclose of the already faulted circuit, not a second initiating fault: the records describe it as returning the circuit to service and the post-event site checks found no defects.

Other lightning-related trips that day are not the initiating event: the Harker–Stella West 275 kV trip at 14:23 and the Blyth–Eccles–Stella West 400 kV trip (16:50:44 in the ESO report narrative, 16:43:25 in ESO's answers to E3C; clock basis not stated, and the two times are not reconciled) both closed again with no power losses or adverse effects recorded, on a day with 12,370 lightning strikes across mainland UK.

quantity.basis: computed: 799 MW before the de-load minus 62 MW after it (S01 event log)

findings.statement: Hornsea One was generating 799 MW at 15:52:33.531Z; its 1B and 1C phases de-loaded between 15:52:33.728Z and 15:52:33.835Z in the operator's log, which is on UTC, i.e. between 16:52:33.728 and 16:52:33.835 BST, while 1A stayed at 62 MW: a reduction of 737 MW.

Little Barford steam turbine ST1C (244 MW) tripped within about 1 s of the fault. The station SOE gives offsets from a datum T = 16:52:34 ± 0.5 s, read as BST: shutdown of the ST control system was initiated at T + 253 ms and the generator breaker opened at T + 1.185 s, i.e. at about 16:52:34.25 and 16:52:35.19 BST, each ± 0.5 s.

Little Barford gas turbine GT1A (210 MW) tripped automatically around a minute after the fault: auto shutdown command at T + 56.583 s and breaker open at T + 57.620 s, i.e. at about 16:53:30.58 and 16:53:31.62 BST (± 0.5 s datum).

findings.derivation: T + 83.897 s = 16:53:57.897 BST; T + 84.613 s = 16:53:58.613 BST (T = 16:52:34 ± 0.5 s); interval between the breaker openings 84.613 s - 57.620 s = 26.993 s (S03 L26-L29), independent of the datum.
findings.statement: Little Barford gas turbine GT1B (187 MW) was tripped manually by operating staff: manual shutdown command at T + 83.897 s and breaker open at T + 84.613 s, i.e. at about 16:53:57.90 and 16:53:58.61 BST (± 0.5 s datum), 26.993 s after the GT1A breaker opened.

quantity.basis: reported station total (S03 L37), equal to the sum of the reported unit outputs at trip

findings.statement: The total generation lost at Little Barford was 641 MW, the sum of the three unit outputs at trip (244 + 210 + 187 MW), which agrees with the published station total.

findings.derivation: Hornsea: S01 UTC readings + 1 h (S01 L6, L40-L43). Little Barford: T + offset (S03 L6-L9, L21-L29); GT1A breaker 57.620 s - 1.185 s = 56.435 s after the ST1C breaker; GT1B breaker 84.613 s - 57.620 s = 26.993 s after GT1A. Fault at 16:52:33.490 BST (R03 L36-L37).
findings.statement: On one clock (BST) the generation losses fall into three groups: the Hornsea de-load (16:52:33.728 to 16:52:33.835, the UTC log + 1 h) and the ST1C trip (T + 1.185 s, about 16:52:35.2 ± 0.5 s) both within about 2 s of the 16:52:33.490 fault; GT1A about 56 s after the ST1C breaker opened (around a minute after the fault); and GT1B about 27 s after GT1A.

The order of the Hornsea de-load and the ST1C trip within the first group cannot be established from these records: the Little Barford datum T carries ± 0.5 s and the operator had not aligned it with the system operator's datum, and the Hornsea log's UTC basis is inferred because the operator labels no clock.

findings.derivation: run_python on the R01 CSV: minimum of frequency_hz over 16:52:45 <= t < 16:53:10 BST (earliest on ties).
findings.statement: First post-fault frequency minimum: 49.083 Hz at 16:52:59 BST, the lowest 1-s sample between 16:52:45 and 16:53:10.

findings.derivation: run_python on the R01 CSV: minimum of frequency_hz over 16:53:20 <= t < 16:54:30 BST.
findings.statement: Event minimum: 48.787 Hz at 16:53:49 BST, the lowest 1-s sample between 16:53:20 and 16:54:30.

findings.derivation: run_python on the R01 CSV: first sample after 16:53:49 with frequency_hz >= 50.
findings.statement: After the event minimum, the first sample at or above 50 Hz is 50.001 Hz at 16:57:16 BST.

findings.derivation: run_python on the R01 CSV: each sample holds its value until the next (no gap exceeds 1 s); sum of holds with frequency_hz < 49 over 16:52:30 <= t < 16:58:00 BST = 33 s. Same window with frequency_hz <= 49: 34 s. Linear interpolation: below 49 Hz from 16:53:40.000 to 16:54:13.964 = 33.964 s.

quantity.basis: count of 1-s samples strictly below 49 Hz x 1 s (zero-order hold)

findings.statement: The frequency was strictly below 49 Hz in 33 consecutive 1-s samples, 16:53:41 to 16:54:13 BST inclusive: 33 s under a zero-order hold (each sample held until the next), with no missing samples between 16:52:30 and 16:58:00. The convention matters at the boundary: 16:53:40 is exactly 49.000 Hz, so counting samples at or below 49 Hz gives 34 s, and linear interpolation between samples gives about 33.96 s.

R01 holds one published value per second (3900 rows, 16:40:00 to 17:44:59 BST) with explicit +01:00 (BST) offsets and no missing or duplicate seconds; the values are unchanged from the NESO dataset, which the publisher corrected in February 2020.

Sub-second behaviour, including the exact instants at which the frequency crossed 49 Hz or 48.8 Hz, cannot be determined from R01's 1-s samples, which record nothing between consecutive samples. The 33 s is a sample-based duration under the stated convention (strictly below 49 Hz, zero-order hold), not a measured crossing-to-crossing time.

Ørsted's investigation report (5 September 2019) concludes that the Hornsea de-load was caused by an unexpected wind farm control system response, due to an insufficiently damped electrical resonance in the sub-synchronous frequency range, triggered by the initial event.

In the operator's account the Hornsea 1B system voltage fell to about 20 kV while the turbines tried to maintain full active power, putting each WTG on 1B and 1C into overcurrent; their protection de-loaded them to 0 MW, while 1A stayed at 62 MW.

The operator reports the outage configuration (one SGT and one OTSUA circuit out of service) as a contributory factor that created a weak internal network, and that its initial suspicion of the Dynamic Reactive Compensator was cleared (the DRC worked as designed and was not the cause).

Ofgem found that the onshore control system operated as expected while the offshore turbine controllers reacted incorrectly to voltage fluctuations on the offshore network; a similar oscillation about ten minutes earlier had not caused de-loading.

The ST1C trip was initiated automatically by a discrepancy between its three speed signals after the point of transmission fault clearance; Ofgem states this as established, the discrepancy having exceeded the control system's tolerance.
After the ST1C trip the plant went into steam bypass operation, steam pressure rose, and GT1A tripped automatically on a high-pressure excursion in the steam bypass system.
With steam pressure still rising, operating staff manually tripped GT1B because of excessive steam pressure and the safety risk.

Not established: why the three ST1C speed signals disagreed. The operator's review of hardware, software, fault handling and diagnostic coverage was ongoing, and Ofgem states that the root cause of the discrepancy has not been established.

Not established: why the steam bypass pressure excursions occurred. The operator gives the GT1A excursion as occurring 'for reasons presently unknown', Ofgem states that the root cause has not been established, and a physical inspection of the bypass system was planned.

Ofgem's preliminary view, given in the absence of an established root cause, is that the anomalous ST1C speed readings and the resulting trip were due to the transmission network fault following the lightning strike.

The operator hypothesises that the UPS units changed over to battery supply because of the disturbance; it does not believe the UPS were related to the trips, and the supply characteristic that caused the changeover was still to be determined.

report.executive_summary:
On 9 August 2019 at 16:52:33.490 BST a single-phase (blue) to earth fault occurred on one Eaton Socon–Wymondley 400 kV circuit, coincident with three lightning strikes recorded at the Wymondley end [F01, F02]. Main protection cleared it in 70 ms at Wymondley Main and 74 ms at Eaton Socon, inside the 80 ms requirement, and delayed auto-reclose restored the circuit at 16:52:53, about 20 s later [F03, F04, F05, F06]. The reclose and the other lightning trips that day were not further initiating events [F07, F08].

Two transmission-connected generators then lost output. All times here are BST: the Hornsea log is on UTC and was converted by adding one hour, and the Little Barford records give offsets from a station datum T = 16:52:34 ± 0.5 s, so their clock times are T + offset and carry that ± 0.5 s. Hornsea One de-loaded from 799 MW to 62 MW (737 MW) between 16:52:33.728 and .835, and Little Barford's steam turbine ST1C (244 MW) tripped within about a second, its breaker opening at about 16:52:35.2 [F10, F11]. Around a minute after the fault GT1A (210 MW) tripped automatically (about 16:53:31.6), and about 27 s later operators tripped GT1B (187 MW) manually (about 16:53:58.6), a station total of 641 MW [F12, F13, F14, F15]. The records support these time groups but not the order of the initial losses, because the Little Barford datum carries ± 0.5 s and was not aligned with the system operator's clock [F16].

In the measured frequency record (R01, 1-s samples, BST offsets) the frequency fell to a first minimum of 49.083 Hz at 16:52:59, then to an event minimum of 48.787 Hz at 16:53:49, and first returned to at least 50 Hz with 50.001 Hz at 16:57:16 [F20, F21, F22]. Counting the 1-s samples strictly below 49 Hz under a zero-order hold gives 33 s (16:53:41 to 16:54:13); because 16:53:40 is exactly 49.000 Hz, an at-or-below count gives 34 s and linear interpolation about 33.96 s [F23]. One-second data cannot show sub-second crossing times [F24, F25].

The trip mechanisms are supported by the operators' and regulator's accounts. At Hornsea, the operator attributes the de-load to an insufficiently damped sub-synchronous resonance in the wind farm control system, which drove the 1B and 1C turbines into overcurrent so that protection de-loaded them; a weak internal network from planned outages contributed, and the initial suspicion of the reactive compensator was cleared [F30, F31, F32, F33]. At Little Barford, ST1C tripped on a discrepancy between three speed signals, GT1A tripped automatically on high steam bypass pressure, and GT1B was tripped manually for excessive steam pressure [F34, F35, F36].

The underlying causes at Little Barford remain unresolved: neither why the speed signals disagreed nor why the bypass pressure rose has been established [F37, F38]. Ofgem's view linking the speed anomaly to the transmission fault, and the operator's UPS changeover hypothesis, are recorded as hypotheses, not findings [F39, F40].

sections.body: The initiating event is the 16:52:33.490 BST single-phase (blue) to earth fault on an Eaton Socon–Wymondley 400 kV circuit, which NGET attributes to lightning; three strikes were recorded at the Wymondley end at 16:52:33 [F01, F02]. R03 reads these times as BST because its sources do not label the clock. Main protection opened the Wymondley end after 70 ms and the Eaton Socon end after 74 ms [F03, F04], within the 80 ms requirement, and the network owner and system operator assess the protection as operating as designed [F05]. Delayed auto-reclose re-energised the circuit at 16:52:53 [F06]; this is the designed reclose, not a second initiating fault [F07]. The Blyth–Eccles–Stella West and Harker–Stella West trips that day closed again without power losses and are not the initiator [F08].

| Initial (about 1-2 s) | Little Barford ST1C | 244 | about 16:52:34.25-16:52:35.19 | SOE datum T + offset, ± 0.5 s [F11] |

| About 27 s later | GT1B (manual) | 187 | about 16:53:58.6 | T + 84.613 s, ± 0.5 s [F13] |

Little Barford lost 641 MW in total [F14]. The grouping is supported [F15]; the order within the initial group is not, because the two clocks are not aligned to better than the ± 0.5 s datum [F16].

sections.body: Computed with run_python from the R01 CSV after checking that the series is strictly increasing in 1-s steps with explicit +01:00 offsets [F24]: first minimum 49.083 Hz at 16:52:59 [F20]; event minimum 48.787 Hz at 16:53:49 [F21]; first sample at or above 50 Hz after it 50.001 Hz at 16:57:16 [F22]. Convention for the time below 49 Hz: samples strictly below 49 Hz, each held until the next sample (zero-order hold), gaps not bridged: 33 samples from 16:53:41 to 16:54:13, i.e. 33 s. The 16:53:40 sample is exactly 49.000 Hz, so an at-or-below count gives 34 s and linear interpolation about 33.96 s [F23]. Threshold crossings between samples are not resolvable from 1-s data [F25].
sections.heading: Frequency minima, recovery and time below 49 Hz

sections.body: Hornsea: control-system resonance leading to turbine overcurrent protection, with a weak internal network as a contributory factor and the DRC cleared [F30, F31, F32, F33]. Little Barford: speed-signal discrepancy (ST1C), automatic trip on bypass pressure (GT1A), manual trip on steam pressure (GT1B) [F34, F35, F36]. Not established, labelled unknown: the cause of the speed-signal discrepancy [F37] and of the pressure excursions [F38]. Labelled hypotheses: Ofgem's preliminary view on the speed readings [F39] and the UPS changeover [F40].
sections.heading: Established trip mechanisms versus unknown causes

sections.body: S01, S03 and S04 are labelled reconstructions; R03 is reconstructed from published records; R01 is a real measured extract. The records use three clock bases: R01 and R03 in BST, the Hornsea log in UTC (an inference stated in its header), and Little Barford offsets from a datum T = 16:52:34 ± 0.5 s read as BST [F10, F11, F16]. Several statements are later, attributed assessments rather than contemporaneous records [F05, F30, F33, F39].
